column5: Joseph serves Potiphar and is set over his household
column6: The commentary uses Yusuf's human rabb as an owner who gives him a good home; Genesis places Joseph as servant in Potiphar's house and then makes him its manager, supplying the matching household relation in the shared Joseph story.

column5: Joseph's master leaves his house and possessions in Joseph's hand
column6: The commentary describes rabb as owner of a house and malik as what a hand possesses; Genesis gives Joseph authority over his master's house while Potiphar retains ownership, sharpening the distinction between a human master's trust and ownership.

column5: Pharaoh's forced labor of Israel
column6: The commentary's Moses scene contrasts being raised in Pharaoh's house with Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel; Exodus describes the same people forced into labor, giving the human domination behind that contrast.

column5: Harsh labor and servitude in Egypt
column6: The commentary's account of Pharaoh enslaving Israel is matched by Exodus's description of bitter labor under Egyptian taskmasters; the narrative adds the grinding work through which human rule humbles its subjects.

column5: Israel released to serve God
column6: The commentary contrasts human enslavement with worship due to God; here God demands that Pharaoh release Israel so the people can serve God, recasting the exodus as a transfer from Pharaoh's forced labor to divine service.

column5: Hebrew עבד for service to God
column6: The commentary labels Arabic ع ب د for both worship and human enslavement; Exodus uses the cognate Hebrew root עבד for Israel's service to God, showing the cultic use of the same Semitic service word in the story of release from forced labor.

column5: A slave chooses to remain with his master
column6: The commentary says human servitude to God begins through creation rather than a slave's choice; this law has a Hebrew slave declare love for his master and refuse release, a concrete human bond chosen after the term of service.

column5: Israelites are God's servants and not human property
column6: The commentary says all people belong to God whether free or enslaved; Leviticus grounds Israel's status as God's servants in the exodus and bars their sale as slaves, limiting human ownership by God's prior claim.

column5: Hebrew עבד for exclusive service
column6: The commentary labels Arabic ع ب د for worship and service and reads 1:5 as service to God alone; Deuteronomy uses the cognate Hebrew root עבד in its command to serve the Lord alone, giving a direct lexical and ethical counterpart.

column5: Collective pledge to serve and obey the Lord
column6: The commentary hears the owned servant speak directly to the owner in the first-person plural; Israel here answers in a collective pledge to serve the Lord and obey his voice, adding a covenantal setting for that spoken allegiance.

column5: The earth and its fullness belong to the Lord
column6: The commentary's malik image includes everything held in the owner's hand; this psalm assigns the earth and all within it to the Lord, extending the property image from household goods to the world.

column5: Bowing and kneeling before the maker
column6: The commentary calls worship the utmost humbling of the servant; the psalm invites worshippers to bow and kneel before their maker, giving bodily posture to its account of submission.

column5: People as sheep of God's hand
column6: The commentary makes the servant God's owned person and places him in the master's house; the psalm calls the worshippers God's people and the sheep of his hand, combining belonging with a shepherd's care.

column5: Every knee bends and every tongue swears
column6: The commentary says every human is already God's servant by creation and that the servant addresses God directly; Isaiah pictures universal bodily submission and confession before God, adding a public, eschatological form of that allegiance.

column5: Hebrew מלך for kingship
column6: The commentary labels Arabic م ل ك for malik as owner and sovereign; Zechariah uses the cognate Hebrew מלך for the Lord's kingship over the whole earth, showing the sovereign sense without importing the commentary's separate property sense.

column5: Aramaic דינא for judgment
column6: The commentary labels Arabic د ي ن and links it to humbling, enslavement, possession, and the Day of Judgment; Daniel's Aramaic cognate root names the court's judgment, directly matching the judgment sense while not supporting those other senses.

column5: Dominion and service of the humanlike figure
column6: The commentary joins malik sovereignty to the servant's worship; Daniel gives everlasting dominion to one like a son of man and says peoples and languages will serve him, a close image of universal service under a ruler with a distinct figure in the vision.

column5: Donkey's burden and the slave's work
column6: The commentary moves from a camel subdued by tar to a humbled human slave; Sirach places fodder, stick, and burden for a donkey beside bread, discipline, and work for a slave, explicitly bringing animal control and human servitude together.

column5: A master assigns a servant work and finds rest
column6: The commentary describes a human owner using a slave's labor and calls the servant humbled by work; Sirach says setting the servant to work gives the master rest, making the labor relation explicit.

column5: Yoke and harness bend a servant's neck
column6: The commentary's common image is one who has been subdued; Sirach describes yoke and harness bending the neck and punishment for a bad servant, offering a concrete Jewish parallel for bodily subjection.

column5: Reciting Shema as accepting heaven's yoke
column6: The commentary reads 1:5 as a spoken acceptance of belonging and obedience to God; this rabbinic ordering says Shema first accepts the yoke of heaven and then the commandments, giving liturgical interpretation to the servant's first-person pledge.

column5: Worship and serve God alone
column6: The commentary's 1:5 makes worship exclusive and defines it through obedient submission; Jesus answers the tempter by directing worship and service to God alone, pairing the two acts in a concrete temptation scene.

column5: One slave cannot serve two masters
column6: The commentary's servant speaks allegiance to one owner; Jesus says a slave cannot serve two masters and contrasts God with wealth, making divided ownership the practical test of exclusive devotion.

column5: A king settles accounts with servants
column6: The commentary joins Malik and Dīn as sovereign and judgment; Jesus begins a parable with a king settling accounts with his servants, giving a household scene in which ownership and reckoning meet.

column5: A debtor and his household sold into slavery
column6: The commentary links Dīn to subduing, enslavement, and possession; in the king's reckoning a debtor is ordered sold with his family and possessions, concretely combining debt judgment with human ownership.

column5: Greatness as becoming a slave
column6: The commentary calls worship the servant's utmost humbling and warns against humans making one another lords; Jesus says the first must become the others' slave, reversing status within a human hierarchy.

column5: The King sits in judgment
column6: The commentary names God malik on the Day of Judgment; Jesus depicts the Son of Man coming in glory and sitting on a throne, giving the judgment scene an enthroned sovereign.

column5: The judge names himself King and assigns inheritance
column6: The commentary names God malik on the Day of Judgment; after nations are gathered and separated, the figure calls himself King and assigns an inheritance, locating kingship in his verdict.

column5: Nations gathered and separated for judgment
column6: The commentary's Day of Judgment includes a sovereign who rules over servants; Jesus gathers all nations before the enthroned figure and separates them as a shepherd separates sheep, adding a universal judgment scene.

column5: Aramaic/Hebrew rabbî as a teacher's title
column6: The commentary's source label ر ب ب explains rabb as an obeyed master and human household owner; John's disciples address Jesus as Rabbi and the Gospel glosses the title as Teacher, showing the Semitic cognate in a teacher-authority setting.

column5: The Lord and Teacher washes his disciples' feet
column6: The commentary distinguishes the owner from the humiliated servant; Jesus explicitly takes the role of teacher and Lord while washing his disciples' feet, making a servant's lowly work the action of the master.

column5: A servant is not greater than the master
column6: The commentary's image depends on the servant's subordination to the owner; Jesus uses the servant/master relation to set the disciples' status after washing their feet, while the scene has already shown the master serving.

column5: Obedience makes one a slave
column6: The commentary links Dīn with obedience and the slave with being humbled; Paul says people become slaves to the one they obey, directly joining obedience to servile status.

column5: Freed from sin and enslaved to God
column6: The commentary says both free and enslaved humans are God's servants by creation; Paul describes people freed from sin and enslaved to God, a specific transformation of status that makes the paradox explicit.

column5: Believers are not their own
column6: The commentary says the human servant belongs to an owner; Paul tells the Corinthians they are not their own because they were bought at a price, giving a direct ownership formulation.

column5: A free person called in Christ is Christ's slave
column6: The commentary says free and enslaved people alike are God's servants; Paul calls the free person who is called by the Lord Christ's slave, making freedom and divine belonging coexist.

column5: Bought with a price, not slaves of humans
column6: The commentary places divine ownership above the human master's claim; Paul says believers were bought with a price and must not become slaves of humans, explicitly limiting human ownership.

column5: The Lord takes a slave's form
column6: The commentary locates humiliation in the servant and says the owner does not undergo humiliation; the Christian hymn says Christ takes a slave's form, a striking reversal in which the one confessed as Lord assumes the servant's station.

column5: The servant-form is expressed as humility and obedience
column6: The commentary defines worship as the utmost humbling and links the servant with obedience; the hymn describes Christ humbling himself and becoming obedient to death, while assigning this path to the exalted figure.

column5: Isaiah's universal bowing applied to Jesus
column6: The commentary says every human belongs to God by creation; Philippians reuses Isaiah's universal knee-bowing image for Jesus, giving the earlier monotheistic passage a specifically Christological reading.

column5: Universal confession that Jesus is Lord
column6: The commentary says worship belongs to the divine owner; Philippians applies Isaiah's universal confession to Jesus as Lord, a Christian interpretation that identifies the honored figure in the universal submission scene.

column5: Earthly masters have a Master in heaven
column6: The commentary links a human owner to the higher owner who rules all; Paul tells masters to act justly because they too have a Master in heaven, limiting household power under divine authority.

column5: Slaves owe honor to human masters
column6: The commentary's B006 gloss describes someone honored as if worshipped; Timothy tells enslaved believers to regard their masters as worthy of honor, adding a household rule that distinguishes human honor from divine worship.

column5: Free people remain God's servants
column6: The commentary says human freedom does not cancel being God's servant; Peter tells believers to live as free people while remaining God's servants, holding both statuses together.

column5: Everyone appears before Christ's judgment seat
column6: The commentary joins malik with the Day of Judgment; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat and receive what is due, adding personal accountability to the sovereign judgment motif.

column5: Creation exists by God's will and worships him
column6: The commentary grounds universal servitude in God's act of creating; heaven's worship in Revelation calls God creator of all things and says they exist by his will, directly linking creation and divine honor.

column5: Every creature worships the throne and the Lamb
column6: The commentary says all who are created come as servants to God; Revelation gives praise from every creature to the throne and the Lamb, extending the universal service image while including the Lamb alongside God.

column5: The dead judged before the throne
column6: The commentary names God malik on the Day of Judgment; Revelation's throne scene opens books and judges the dead according to their deeds, a direct eschatological counterpart.

column5: God's servants worship at the throne
column6: The commentary calls the servant the owned person who worships God; Revelation's final vision says God's servants worship him at his throne, joining servant identity, worship, and the divine household.

column5: Moses raised in Pharaoh's household
column6: The commentary pairs Pharaoh's claim to have raised Moses with his enslavement of Israel; Exodus says Pharaoh's daughter raises Moses as her son in the palace, preserving the family-raising detail while locating it specifically with the daughter.

column5: Creation, belonging, and the ketiv/qere
column6: The commentary grounds universal servitude in being created; this verse names God as maker and Israel as his people and pasture's flock. WLC's ketiv reads ולא אנחנו, while the qere reads ולו אנחנו, so explicit wording that the people are God's belongs to the qere.

column5: All creation as God's servants
column6: The commentary says people are God's servants by being brought into existence; the psalm says the created order stands by God's ordinances and calls all things his servants, extending the service image beyond humanity.

column5: Bit and bridle restrain horse and mule
column6: The commentary's B005 gloss makes a subdued camel an image of submission; this proverb says an uncomprehending person must be restrained like a horse or mule with bit and bridle, while using the image as a warning against stubbornness rather than praising domination.

column5: Creation serves its maker
column6: The commentary says all humans come to God as servants because he created them; Wisdom says creation itself serves its maker, extending the creator-servant relation from humanity to the natural order.

column5: Work imposed to prevent idleness
column6: The commentary explains the slave through work that lowers him; Sirach commands work for the servant and treats idleness as a danger, adding an ancient household ethic to the labor image.

column5: Serving God without seeking a reward
column6: The commentary stresses worship as a servant's status and obedience, not merely a feeling; Antigonus teaches that servants should serve their master without serving for a reward, adding a motive-focused Jewish reading of divine service.

column5: The Elect One enthroned to judge sinners
column6: The commentary joins Malik with the Day of Judgment; Enoch seats the Elect One on a throne of glory and describes the destruction of sinners before him, an apocalyptic expansion of enthroned authority as judicial rule.

column5: The Son of Man serves rather than receives service
column6: The commentary presents the master as owner and the servant as the one humbled; Jesus describes the Son of Man as serving and giving his life, placing service in the role of the exalted figure.

column5: Rabbi title and shared brotherhood
column6: The commentary warns against taking one another as lords; Jesus tells disciples not to seek the title Rabbi because they are brothers and have one teacher, a specific Christian limit on human religious authority.

column5: Human beings refuse worship and point to the Creator
column6: The commentary calls God the one worshipped and treats humans as created servants; Paul and Barnabas reject a crowd's worship, identify themselves as human, and direct it to the living Creator, clarifying why a human must not take divine honor.

column5: The Creator gives life and is not served from need
column6: The commentary grounds human service in being created and treats God as owner; Paul says the world's maker is not served by human hands as though needy, because he gives life and all things, distinguishing worship from supplying a master's lack.

column5: Servants see God's face
column6: The commentary pictures the slave as belonging to the owner's house; Revelation promises God's servants access to his face and name, adding intimate presence to the household relation.

column5: A road prepared in the wilderness
column6: The commentary's road is made passable by being trampled and subdued; Isaiah calls for a way prepared in the wilderness, a specific road-making image that may illuminate the comparison, though the Hebrew passage does not use the commentary's Arabic root.

column5: Uneven ground leveled for a road
column6: The commentary glosses the road as flattened and made traversable; Isaiah describes valleys raised and mountains lowered as the route is made level, an adjacent but distinct image of making a road passable.

column5: The Lord identifies himself as Israel's redeemer from slavery
column6: The commentary grounds human belonging to God in creation and contrasts divine ownership with Pharaoh's human enslavement; the covenant begins by naming the Lord who brought Israel out of a slave-house, making exclusive allegiance a response to liberation.

column5: No bowing to or serving other gods
column6: The commentary reads 1:5 as exclusive worship of the one owner; this command prohibits bowing to other gods and serving them, specifying the covenantal acts excluded by that allegiance.

column5: Hebrew דִּין for judging his people and servants
column6: The commentary labels Arabic د ي ن and connects it to both the Day of Judgment and the servant's subjection; Deuteronomy uses the cognate Hebrew root for the Lord judging his people and showing compassion to his servants, pairing judgment with the servant relation.

column5: Israel challenged to choose whom to follow
column6: The commentary hears a first-person commitment to worship one alone; Elijah confronts Israel's divided allegiance between the Lord and Baal, placing exclusive service in a public contest over rival gods.

column5: Humans given rule over livestock
column6: The commentary opens with an owner of animals and then says humans themselves are God's servants by creation; the psalm places sheep, cattle, and wild animals under human rule, showing delegated animal mastery beneath divine creation.

column5: The worshipper calls himself God's servant and recalls released bonds
column6: The commentary makes the servant speak directly to the owner; the psalmist calls himself the Lord's servant and says God has loosed his bonds, adding a first-person prayer of servitude after deliverance.

column5: Servants watch their masters' hands
column6: The commentary describes the owned servant's posture before a master; the psalm compares worshippers' gaze toward God to the eyes of male and female servants fixed on their masters' hands, giving a precise domestic image for dependence in prayer.

column5: Israel formed by God and called his own
column6: The commentary says the human servant belongs to God by being created; Isaiah addresses Jacob as formed by God and says he is God's, joining creation, personal address, and possession in one promise.

column5: Every life belongs to God in a judgment context
column6: The commentary joins God's malik status to human servitude; Ezekiel declares every life God's and then speaks of individual accountability, connecting divine ownership with judgment rather than human possession.

column5: Exiles refuse royal demand to worship an image
column6: The commentary's 1:5 makes worship exclusive despite human power; the Judeans refuse the king's command to worship his image, showing allegiance to God under an imperial test.

column5: Servants say they have done their duty
column6: The commentary's speaker says in the first-person plural that they worship and explains worship as obedient submission; Jesus has servants conclude that they have only done their duty, giving a concrete household form for service without claiming merit.

column5: Moses faithful as a servant in God's house
column6: The commentary pictures a human servant in the owner's house; Hebrews calls Moses faithful as a servant within God's house, placing the Mosaic figure in a divine household and clarifying the servant's subordinate role.

column5: The Son stands over the house
column6: The commentary distinguishes the owner from the servant who belongs in the owner's house; Hebrews contrasts Moses the servant with Christ as Son over God's house, making household status the basis of a theological distinction.

column5: One lawgiver and judge can save or destroy
column6: The commentary says God alone is the owner and judge while humans must not make one another lords; James names one lawgiver and judge able to save and destroy, explicitly grounding the limit on judging others in God's singular authority.

column5: Earthly kings fall before the enthroned Son of Man
column6: The commentary links sovereign rule to the humiliation of servants before their owner; Enoch depicts kings and powerful people falling before the enthroned Son of Man and seeking mercy, extending the image of universal subordination into Jewish apocalyptic judgment.

column5: The pierced ear recalls that Israel belongs to God
column6: The commentary says the servant is God's by creation and describes human beings as enslaved by other people; this rabbinic interpretation of the permanent Hebrew slave's pierced ear says the ear heard that Israel belongs to God and should not become a slave to slaves, directly limiting human ownership.

column5: A Hebrew servant leaves after six years
column6: The commentary describes humans as God's servants by creation, not by an initial choice; this law limits a human master's claim to six years and requires release in the seventh, distinguishing temporary human servitude from the creator's prior claim.

column5: Release of a servant grounded in Israel's own slavery
column6: The commentary develops the human owner and enslaved person's status; Deuteronomy requires a master to release a Hebrew servant generously because Israel remembers being enslaved in Egypt and redeemed by God, adding an ethical consequence to divine ownership.

column5: Disciples no longer called slaves but friends
column6: The commentary presents the human as God's owned servant by creation; Jesus says his disciples are no longer slaves who lack knowledge of the master's affairs but friends who have been told what he heard, adding a Christian shift from subordination to disclosed intimacy.

column5: A free speaker makes himself a slave to others
column6: The commentary says the servant's status is not initiated by choice because it follows creation; Paul says that though free he made himself a slave to all, offering a contrasting voluntary form of service for others.

column5: Human creation directed toward God
column6: The commentary treats being created as the ground of belonging to God; Augustine opens by interpreting human creation as oriented toward God and rest in God, adding an account of the human longing that accompanies creaturely dependence.
